question: Who sets the prices of phone calls, video visits and commissary items in prisons and jails, and can the facility or sheriff keep a commission?

groups: telephone services to incarcerated individual facilities
items available for purchase at a commissary
goods and services that benefit the general incarcerated individual population
credited to or disbursed from an account

gold_sections.why: The Commissioner's annual report (due October 31) must state, for each correctional facility in the Division of Correction, the average cost of telephone calls (including calls to medical providers), video calls and commissary items; the only Maryland statute that names these prices, and it reports them rather than setting them. It does not reach county jails, Patuxent or the Division of Pretrial Detention and Services facilities.
In Title 3, 'Division' means the Division of Correction, which limits the 3-207 cost report to Division of Correction facilities.

A 'telephone company' includes a public service company that owns telephone lines to communicate telephone services to incarcerated individual facilities (1-101(nn)(1)(iii)), and telephone companies are public service companies (1-101(z)); this reaches line-owning carriers serving the facilities, not every calling vendor.

To the full extent federal law allows, the Public Service Commission has jurisdiction over each public service company operating a utility business in the State; federal prison-phone law can therefore limit or override the Commission's role.
Defines 'just and reasonable rate' (no violation of the article, consistent with the public good, and a reasonable return), the standard the Commission applies when setting rates.
The Public Service Commission may set a just and reasonable rate of a public service company as a maximum rate, minimum rate, or both.
A public service company must charge just and reasonable rates for the regulated services it renders.

Public service companies file tariff schedules of their rates and charges with the Commission; discretionary and competitive telephone services are exempt, the Commission may excuse telephone companies with 20,000 or fewer subscribers, and it may regulate untariffed telephone services by order or regulation.
The Commission may regulate a telephone company through alternative forms of regulation, including price regulation.

Defines VoIP service as real-time two-way voice over Internet protocol that requires a broadband connection from the user's location; whether a given prison calling platform meets this definition is not settled by the text.
The Commission has no jurisdiction over service that meets the 8-601 VoIP definition, including tariffs, but 8-602(b)(6) keeps its jurisdiction over circuit switched local exchange access service.
Each Division of Correction facility keeps reserve and spending accounts for every incarcerated individual, and the Commissioner's regulations set what may be credited to or disbursed from them.

Each State correctional facility has an incarcerated individual welfare fund, usable only for goods and services that benefit the general incarcerated population as Department regulations define; the section creates the fund and limits its use but does not say what revenue goes into it.
The Comptroller pays out money from each State welfare fund as approved in the State budget.

Each local correctional facility may establish a welfare fund, usable only for goods and services benefiting the general incarcerated population as the managing official's regulations define; it does not say what revenue goes into the fund.
The county chief financial officer (or, in Dorchester County, the CFO or a designated managing official) pays out local welfare fund money as approved in the county budget.

'Managing official' includes a sheriff; 'local correctional facility' means one run by one or more counties or a municipal corporation; 'State correctional facility' includes Patuxent, the Baltimore City Detention Center and Baltimore's centralized booking facility, so Baltimore City's pretrial jail is a State facility.
Local jails and Division of Correction facilities must have a written policy providing menstrual hygiene products at no cost, so access to them does not depend on commissary purchases.
Extends the free menstrual hygiene products rule to the Patuxent Institution, which 9-616 does not cover.

nuggets.text: The Commissioner of Correction's annual report must state, for each Division of Correction facility, the average cost of telephone calls (including calls to medical providers), video calls, and commissary items such as feminine hygiene products, toiletries and medications.
nuggets.quote: the annual cost of living for incarcerated individuals, including the average cost of: (i) telephone calls, including calls to medical providers; (ii) video calls; and (iii) items available for purchase at a commissary, including: 1. feminine hygiene products; 2. toiletries; and 3. medications

nuggets.text: The Commissioner submits that report to the Secretary of Public Safety and Correctional Services and the Governor on or before October 31 each year (the Governor then sends it to the General Assembly).
nuggets.quote: On or before October 31 of each year, the Commissioner shall submit an annual report to the Secretary and the Governor

nuggets.text: A company that owns telephone lines to carry telephone service to incarcerated individual facilities is a 'telephone company' under the Public Utilities Article.

nuggets.quote: the chief financial officer for the county shall pay out money from each fund as approved in the county budget

nuggets.text: Local jails and Division of Correction facilities must have a written policy providing menstrual hygiene products at no cost to female incarcerated individuals on admission, routinely and on request (the Patuxent Institution has the same rule under 4-214).
nuggets.quote: Each correctional facility shall have a written policy and procedure in place requiring menstrual hygiene products to be provided at no cost to a female incarcerated individual

office.value: Public Service Commission, to the extent federal law allows, may set just and reasonable maximum or minimum rates for telephone companies that own lines serving incarcerated individual facilities
Commissioner of Correction reports the average cost of phone calls, video calls and commissary items at Division of Correction facilities to the Secretary and the Governor

answer: No downloaded Maryland statute sets prices for prison or jail phone calls, video calls or commissary goods, or expressly bans or allows a commission for a facility or sheriff. A company owning lines that serve incarcerated individual facilities is a telephone company [N3]. As far as federal law allows, the Public Service Commission oversees it [N4]: it can set just and reasonable maximum or minimum rates [N5], the company must charge just and reasonable rates [N16] and file tariffs [N6], but VoIP service is outside its reach [N7]. The Commissioner of Correction reports by October 31 each year [N2] the average cost of phone calls, video calls and commissary items at each Division of Correction facility [N1], and regulates what may be credited to or taken from prisoners' accounts [N18]. Every State correctional facility, including Baltimore City's State-run detention center and central booking [N17], has a welfare fund [N8]; a local jail may create one [N11]. Fund money may buy only goods and services benefiting the general incarcerated population, as Department regulations [N9] or the jail's managing official [N12], possibly the sheriff [N13], define, and is paid out under the budget by the Comptroller [N10] or the county's chief financial officer [N14]. The code does not say what revenue, such as commissary profits or phone commissions, goes into these funds. Menstrual hygiene products must be free [N15]. Federal law (47 U.S.C. 276 and FCC rules) governs rate caps and site commissions for incarcerated people's phone and video calls.

out_of_corpus.where: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services procurement contracts for inmate calling, video visitation/tablets and commissary services (State procurement under the State Finance and Procurement Article) and each local jail's vendor contracts

out_of_corpus.what: Rate caps and site-commission rules for incarcerated people's communications services (audio and video, interstate and intrastate)
out_of_corpus.where: 47 U.S.C. 276 as amended by the Martha Wright-Reed Just and Reasonable Communications Act of 2022; FCC rules at 47 CFR Part 64, Subpart FF, set by the 2024 IPCS Order (FCC 24-75) and revised by the 2025 IPCS Order (FCC 25-75, adopted October 28, 2025, WC Docket Nos. 23-62 and 12-375), which replaced the 2024 caps with higher interim caps and kept the rule that providers may not pay site commissions; check the current rules, compliance dates and any court challenges

local_option: Each local correctional facility (one operated by one or more counties or by a municipal corporation, Correctional Services 1-101(l)) may establish an incarcerated individual welfare fund (11-902(a)); its managing official, who may be an administrator, director, warden, superintendent or sheriff (1-101(m)), adopts the regulations defining what the fund may buy (11-902(b)); the county's chief financial officer pays out the money as approved in the county budget, or in Dorchester County the CFO or a managing official the county designates (11-904). Baltimore City's detention center and central booking facility are State correctional facilities (1-101(q)(2)), so this local option does not apply to them. Phone, video and commissary prices and any commission terms at local jails come from local vendor contracts that the corpus does not address, and the corpus does not say who signs them.
notes: Correctional Services 10-503 and 11-903 (the sections between the welfare-fund creation and pay-out sections, which likely address what money goes into the State and local welfare funds; their content is not verified) are missing from the downloaded open-us-law corpus, so this reference cannot say from the corpus whether commissary profits or phone commissions must be deposited in those funds. A correct answer should not claim either a statutory commission ban or a statutory authorization, and should not say that commissions flow into the welfare funds: 10-502 and 11-902 only create the funds and limit their use. Public Utilities 1-101(nn)(1)(iii) treats a company that owns telephone lines serving incarcerated individual facilities as a telephone company, and 1-101(z) makes telephone companies public service companies, so PSC rate power (4-102, 4-201, 4-301) and tariff filing (4-202(a)) reach line-owning carriers' intrastate prison phone service, subject to the federal-law limit in 2-112(a)(1); 4-202(c) exempts discretionary and competitive (Basket 4 and 5) telephone services from tariff filing, lets the Commission excuse small carriers and lets it regulate untariffed services by order or regulation. 8-602(a) removes service that meets the 8-601 VoIP definition (two-way voice over Internet protocol requiring a broadband connection from the user's location) from PSC jurisdiction, while 8-602(b)(6) keeps jurisdiction over circuit switched local exchange access service; whether a prison calling platform is VoIP service is not settled by the text. No statute addresses video-call pricing beyond the 3-207(a)(7)(ii) reporting item, and 3-207 covers only Division of Correction facilities (3-101(c)), not county jails, Patuxent or the Division of Pretrial Detention and Services facilities. Baltimore City's detention center and central booking facility are State correctional facilities under 1-101(q)(2), so they have State welfare funds under 10-502. Menstrual hygiene products: 9-616 covers local jails and Division of Correction facilities, 4-214 covers Patuxent; neither names the Pretrial Detention facilities. 3-609 requires reserve and spending accounts for each Division of Correction prisoner, with the Commissioner's regulations setting what may be credited or disbursed; the statute does not itself mention phone or commissary charges. 10-501 and 11-901 (defining 'fund' by cross-reference) were left out of the gold sections because they add no substance. The $4 medical visit fees (Correctional Services 2-118, 5-405, 11-203) are copays, not commissary prices. Human Services 9-237(c)(8) requires juvenile detention standards to address children's telephone use, and 9-614.1(d)(2) gives minors in restrictive housing the same phone access as others, without addressing price. Courts and Judicial Proceedings 2-313(c)(2) (county pays the sheriff's office telephone expenses) is about the sheriff's own office phones, not incarcerated people's calls. The FCC history in out_of_corpus was checked by web search on 2026-10-10 (FCC 25-75 released November 6, 2025); confirm against the current FCC docket before relying on it.
